article.title: Fitzpatrick Skin Type Test: 4-Question Quiz & Guide

article.h1: Fitzpatrick Skin Type Test: A Simple Self-Quiz and What the Result Means
article.body_html:
A Fitzpatrick skin type test sorts you into one of six types (I to VI) based on how your skin reacts to sun: whether it burns, whether it tans, and how much. Below is a short self-quiz, plain-language descriptions of each type, and a clear explanation of why the result is not your skin tone, undertone or foundation shade.

What the Fitzpatrick scale is (and what it isn't)

A six-type scale based on how skin reacts to sun

The Fitzpatrick scale was developed in the 1970s by dermatologist Thomas Fitzpatrick. It groups people by their typical reaction to sun exposure, from skin that burns easily and barely tans (Type I) to skin that very rarely burns and has deep natural pigmentation (Type VI). It is a rough sorting tool, not a precise measurement.

Why it isn't a skin tone, undertone or makeup shade chart

The scale describes sun reaction, not how your skin looks. It says nothing about whether your undertone is warm, cool or neutral, and it does not tell you which foundation, blush or clothing colors suit you. Two people can share a type and look quite different.

A note up front: educational only

This article is educational and cosmetic in focus. It is not medical advice, and no quiz can diagnose anything about your skin. If you have a skin concern, see a dermatologist or doctor.

Before you take the test: how to answer fairly

Think about your natural baseline, not your current tan

Answer for your skin as it is after a winter of covering up, not after a beach holiday. A current tan, or one unusual sunburn, can skew the result.

Recall past reactions; don't test yourself in the sun

Base your answers on what has happened in the past, such as the first long day outdoors in a season without sunscreen. Please do not expose your skin to the sun on purpose to find out. If you can't remember, answer for the most typical reaction you've noticed, or leave the question and rely on the others.

Answer from experience rather than guessing

If you're unsure, ask someone who has seen you after a day outside. Your own memory of how sore or pink you got is usually better than what you assume about your skin color.

A simple Fitzpatrick skin type self-test

This is a simplified, informal quiz written for this guide, not a clinical tool. Pick one answer per question and note its points (0 to 4).

Question 1: What is your natural, unexposed skin color?

  • Very pale or ivory: 0
  • Fair: 1
  • Light to medium: 2
  • Olive or medium brown: 3
  • Deep brown to very deep brown: 4

Question 2: What usually happens after 30 to 60 minutes of midday sun with no protection?

  • Painful burn, possibly blistering or peeling: 0
  • Burns and usually peels: 1
  • Mild burn: 2
  • Rarely burns: 3
  • Almost never burns: 4

Question 3: How easily do you tan afterward, and how deep does it go?

  • Don't tan, just turn red or freckle: 0
  • Tan lightly and slowly: 1
  • Tan gradually to light brown: 2
  • Tan easily to a moderate brown: 3
  • Tan quickly and deeply: 4

Question 4: How does your skin react after repeated exposure over several days?

  • Always burns first: 0
  • Usually burns before tanning: 1
  • Sometimes burns: 2
  • Rarely burns: 3
  • Almost never burns: 4

How to score your answers

Add up your four scores (0 to 16):

  • 0 to 2: Type I
  • 3 to 5: Type II
  • 6 to 8: Type III
  • 9 to 11: Type IV
  • 12 to 14: Type V
  • 15 to 16: Type VI

Treat the result as a rough guess. Sun reaction matters more than skin color here, so if Question 2 and Question 3 point to a different type than Question 1, trust those two.

The six Fitzpatrick types in plain language

Types I and II: burn easily, tan little or not at all

Type I typically burns almost every time and does not tan. Type II burns easily and may tan a little. Both usually have lighter natural skin, though skin color alone doesn't decide it.

Types III and IV: burn sometimes or rarely, tan gradually to easily

Type III sometimes burns and tans gradually to a light or moderate brown. Type IV burns rarely and tans fairly easily. These types cover a wide range of looks, including light-olive and medium-brown skin.

Types V and VI: rarely or almost never burn, deeper natural pigmentation

Type V rarely burns and tans readily. Type VI very rarely burns and has the deepest natural pigmentation. Rarely burning does not mean never, and it does not mean sun protection is optional.

What to do if you fall between two types

This is common. Because the scale is a rough grouping, people often sit on a border, such as between III and IV. Note both types and, if you need an accurate answer for a health reason, ask a dermatologist or doctor rather than relying on an online quiz.

Fitzpatrick type vs skin tone vs undertone

A quick comparison: what each measures and what it's used for

TermWhat it describesTypically used for
Fitzpatrick typeHow skin reacts to sun (burning and tanning)A rough, self-reported sun-reaction grouping
Skin tone (depth)How light or deep your skin looksFoundation depth, concealer, bronzer
UndertoneThe warm, cool or neutral hue beneath the surfaceFoundation match, blush, jewelry metals, clothing colors

Why two people with the same type can look quite different

One Type III person may have a golden, warm undertone and another a cool, pink one. Their sun reactions are similar, but a peachy blush and gold jewelry might flatter the first, while a rosy blush and silver might suit the second.

Where to go to find your depth and undertone instead

For color and makeup decisions, use our guides to finding your skin tone depth and undertone and simple undertone tests.

What your result can and can't tell you

It's a rough, self-reported sorting tool

Your answers depend on memory, past sun habits, climate and whether you used sunscreen. That makes the result approximate.

Its limits, including for darker skin tones

The scale groups a very wide range of skin into a few types, and it is often criticized for not capturing the variation within deeper skin tones. Types V and VI in particular cover a lot of ground, so the number is not a full description of anyone.

Every type needs sun protection; any skin concern belongs with a professional

A higher number does not mean you are safe in the sun. Widely accepted basics, such as sunscreen, shade and protective clothing, apply to every type. If you notice a new or changing spot, have a skin concern, or take medication that makes you sun-sensitive, see a dermatologist or doctor instead of relying on a quiz.

What to use for makeup and color choices instead

Depth and undertone for foundation, concealer and blush

Match foundation to your depth first, then fine-tune for undertone. Warm undertones often suit terracotta or peach blush; cool undertones often suit rose or berry; neutral undertones can wear both.

Vein, jewelry and white-vs-cream tests as starting points

Greenish veins, gold jewelry that looks natural, and cream looking better than stark white tend to suggest warm. Blue or purple veins, silver jewelry, and crisp white tend to suggest cool. These are hints, not proof, so check them against several tests.

Using natural-light photos to compare shades

Stand facing a window, hold the camera at eye level and skip filters. Compare shades against your jaw and neck, not just your cheek. For more on previewing looks, see our makeup virtual try-on guide.

Where a cosmetic AI check can fit in

FitCheck AI does not determine your Fitzpatrick type, assess sun sensitivity, or give skincare advice. What it can do is help with the cosmetic follow-up. The live skin analysis uses your camera to give an AI skin overview with cosmetic beauty suggestions, which you can read alongside your own depth and undertone notes. For best results, face natural light, hold the camera at eye level and avoid filters.

The app also has an AI makeup assistant and a live virtual makeup try-on, so you can preview something like a lipstick shade on your own face. For outfits, color match feedback can act as a second opinion. All of it is a starting point, not an objective or professional assessment. The AI feedback is not medical advice, so please see a dermatologist or doctor for any skin concern.

faqs.question: Can I take a Fitzpatrick test from a photo?
faqs.answer: Not reliably. The scale is based on how your skin reacts to sun over time, which a photo can't show, and lighting and filters change how skin looks. A photo can help with cosmetic choices like shade and undertone, but not with your sun-reaction type.

faqs.question: Is the Fitzpatrick scale the same as my skin tone?
faqs.answer: No. The scale describes burning and tanning, while skin tone describes how light or deep your skin looks, and undertone is the warm, cool or neutral hue beneath. Use depth and undertone for makeup and clothing colors.

faqs.question: Does a higher type number mean I'm safe in the sun?
faqs.answer: No. Higher types tend to burn less often, but any skin can be damaged by the sun. Sunscreen, shade and protective clothing are widely recommended for every type.

faqs.question: Can the result change over time?
faqs.answer: Your self-assessed type is meant to describe your typical natural reaction, so it shouldn't swing with a seasonal tan. Your answers may shift if you remember more accurately, and some medications can change sun sensitivity, so ask a doctor if that applies to you.

faqs.question: Should I ask a dermatologist for my type?
faqs.answer: If you need an answer for a health reason, such as a skin concern, a new or changing spot, or sun-sensitive medication, yes. A dermatologist or doctor can assess your skin properly, which an online quiz cannot do.

failures: factual_issues:The self-made scoring system is internally inconsistent. Question 1 (skin color) makes up 25% of the total score, yet the article says skin color doesn't decide Fitzpatrick type and that sun reaction

factual_issues: The self-made scoring system is internally inconsistent. Question 1 (skin color) makes up 25% of the total score, yet the article says skin color doesn't decide Fitzpatrick type and that sun reaction matters more. The advice to 'trust Q2 and Q3' over Q1 is not built into the scoring, so readers can't apply it consistently.

Questions 2 and 4 are near-duplicates (both use 'Rarely burns' and 'Almost never burns'), so burning is double-weighted. The Q1 option 'Olive or medium brown: 3' pushes many olive-skinned people who sometimes burn toward Type IV or V. The 0-2/3-5/6-8/9-11/12-14/15-16 cutoffs are arbitrary and not derived from the standard Fitzpatrick questionnaire. The 'informal' disclaimer reduces the problem but does not remove it, since the headline deliverable is a 'Fitzpatrick skin type test' whose results may misclassify people.
review.notes: Strengths: the article matches informational intent. It has a clear quiz, type descriptions, a Fitzpatrick vs skin tone vs undertone table, and honest limits, including criticism of the scale for darker skin. Sun-safety and dermatologist referrals are appropriate, and it tells readers not to sun-test themselves. App claims are restrained and consistent with APP_FACTS: it states the app does not determine Fitzpatrick type, and it limits the skin analysis to cosmetic suggestions. Fix: redesign the quiz so it reflects sun reaction (for example, drop or reduce the skin-color question, or replace it with eye/hair color and freckling questions, and remove the duplication between Q2 and Q4). Align the 'trust Q2 and Q3' instruction with the scoring, or link to or mirror the standard questionnaire. Minor: 'after a winter of covering up' is hemisphere-specific. Confirm that the internal links resolve.
